title: Transmission-Based Precautions

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Standard Precautions are the seatbelt you buckle every single time you get in a car, no exceptions, no matter who is driving. Transmission-Based Precautions are the extra gear you add when the trip is riskier: a helmet, pads, a roll cage. Nobody unbuckles the seatbelt in order to put the helmet on. That is what 'in addition to' means in CDC's wording, and it is why identifying a pathogen never lets you drop the baseline.

### Question 2

Ask how a germ gets a ride to the next person. Some hitchhike on hands, bed rails, and doorknobs, which is Contact. Some ride heavy spit-drops that arc out of a cough and land within a few feet, which is Droplet. Some float like campfire smoke and drift far from where they started, which is Airborne. The categories are named after the ride, not after the germ or the body system it attacks, so once you know how something travels you already know its category.

### Question 3

Contact germs travel by touch, so you cover the two things that do the touching: your hands and your clothes. Gloves handle the hands, and a gown handles the front of your uniform, which brushes the bed rail, the mattress, and the IV pole without you noticing. It is like painting a room: you put on the gloves and old clothes before you start, not after paint is already on your sleeve. And you take them off inside the room so the paint does not ride into the hallway with you.

### Question 4

Picture two different sprays. A garden hose throws heavy drops that arc out and hit the ground a few feet away, and a shield held in front of you blocks those. That shield is the surgical mask. Now picture campfire smoke: it drifts, curls around corners, and slips through any gap, so a shield with loose edges is useless. You need something that seals tight to your face and filters the tiny bits, and someone has to verify the seal on your particular face. That verification is fit testing.

### Question 5

A negative-pressure room is a room that inhales. Air slides in from the hallway under the door and never sneaks back out, and the air pulled from the room is blown outside the building or run through a HEPA filter that traps the particles. Think of a range hood that pulls smoke straight out instead of letting it wander through the house. Notice who this protects: everyone outside. Inside, the air is still smoky, which is exactly why the respirator stays on.

### Question 6

Match the barrier to the vehicle. Contact germs move like glitter, ending up on your hands, your sleeve, the bed rail, and the doorknob, so you cover hands and clothes with gloves and a gown. Droplet germs move like sneeze-spray that arcs out and lands within a few feet, so you put a barrier in front of your face and keep some distance. If you catch yourself memorizing which gear goes with which disease, back up and ask how the germ is traveling; the gear follows from that.

### Question 7

Pressure just tells you which way the air is being pushed. Negative pressure makes the room inhale; positive pressure makes it exhale. Set an isolation room to exhale and every door swing sends a puff of contaminated air into the hallway, like aiming a fan at the doorway of a smoky room instead of at the window. Here is the part students miss: an N95 protects only the person wearing it. It does nothing for the family sitting in the waiting room down the hall.

### Question 8

Sort by how each germ gets around and the pairings settle themselves. TB rides tiny particles that hang in the air like smoke, so Airborne. Flu and whooping cough ride bigger cough-drops that fall within a few feet, so Droplet. Norovirus rides hands and surfaces touched after vomiting or diarrhea, so Contact. Each wrong pairing here is a barrier aimed at a route the germ does not actually use, which is precisely how an outbreak gets started while everyone believes they are protected.

### Question 9

There are two places to stop a problem: at the source, or at every person downstream. Masking the patient stops it at the source, like putting a lid on a pot so steam never fills the kitchen, instead of handing everyone in the house an umbrella. That is source control, and it is why the corridor full of staff does not need respirators. The mask on the patient is an ordinary surgical mask, because its job is catching what comes out, not filtering what goes in.

### Question 10

C. difficile can wrap itself in a hard shell and become a spore, essentially an armored seed that shrugs off what kills ordinary bacteria. Alcohol gel cannot crack that shell, but soap and running water physically scrub the spores loose and rinse them away, which is removal rather than killing. The same logic applies to the room: an ordinary wipe leaves spores on the bed rail, so a bleach-type sporicidal cleaner is needed. Everything else on this list is routine Contact Precautions; the spore-specific steps are the C. diff signature.

### Question 11

Nobody waits for the fire department to confirm a real fire before leaving the building; the alarm is enough to act on. A cluster of symptoms is that alarm. Act and be wrong, and the cost is a few days in a special room for one patient. Wait and be right, and everyone who walked past that doorway was breathing unprotected the whole time. Start on the syndrome, then stop when the test clears the patient. Contact Precautions would be the wrong alarm entirely, since gown and gloves do nothing about air.

### Question 12

Chickenpox has two travel routes: it drifts through the air from the airway, and it sits in the fluid inside every blister, ready to move on hands and sleeves. Two roads in means two roadblocks, so the respirator and negative-pressure room close the air route while gown and gloves close the touch route. Closing only one is locking the front door and leaving the back door open. Whenever a pathogen has more than one route, you stack the categories rather than picking the scarier-sounding one.
